items.title: The 1991 Crisis and the LPG Reforms
items.body:
## In one line

In 1991 India nearly ran out of foreign money to pay for imports, and the rescue reshaped the whole economy through the **LPG reforms**. Asked for the crisis cause, the gold pledge and who led the reforms.

## Why the crisis happened

By 1991 India faced a severe **balance of payments crisis**:

- **Foreign exchange reserves** had fallen to about **US$1.2 billion — barely 2–3 weeks of import cover**.
- **Twin deficits**: large fiscal deficit and current-account/trade deficit; ballooning **external debt**.
- **Trigger**: the **Gulf War (1990–91)** spiked oil prices and cut remittances from the Gulf.

## The response

- India pledged **gold** to raise forex (RBI airlifted ~47 tonnes to the Bank of England; ~20 tonnes to UBS) and secured an **IMF bailout**.
- PM **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and FM **Dr. Manmohan Singh** launched the **LPG reforms** (New Economic Policy).

## LPG = Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation

| Pillar | Core idea |
|---|---|
| **Liberalisation** | Free market forces — abolish industrial licensing, cut controls |
| **Privatisation** | Reduce state's role — disinvest in PSEs |
| **Globalisation** | Integrate with world economy — trade, FDI, FTAs |

Reforms are also grouped as **stabilisation** (short-term BoP/inflation correction) and **structural** (long-term efficiency-raising) measures.

## Terms explained

- **Balance of payments (BoP) crisis** — when a country cannot pay for its imports or debts in foreign currency.
- **Import cover** — how many weeks of imports the forex reserves can pay for (1991: just 2–3 weeks).
- **LPG** — Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation.
- **IMF bailout** — emergency loan from the International Monetary Fund, with reform conditions.

## TL;DR

- 1991 forex reserves fell to ~US$1.2 bn, about 2–3 weeks of import cover, triggering a BoP crisis.
- Causes: high fiscal/trade deficits, rising external debt, Gulf-War oil-price spike and falling remittances.
- India pledged gold (RBI airlifted ~47 t to Bank of England) and took an IMF bailout.
- LPG reforms launched by PM P.V. Narasimha Rao and FM Dr. Manmohan Singh (1991).
- LPG = Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation; also framed as stabilisation vs structural reforms.

items.title: Key Reform Measures (Industry, Trade, Finance)
items.body:
## In one line

This note lists the **concrete steps** of the 1991 reforms across industry, trade and finance — delicensing, disinvestment, SEBI and SEZs. Asked for which controls were removed and when.

## Liberalisation measures

- **Abolition of industrial licensing** for most industries (except a few strategic/security sectors).
- **MRTP Act amended (1991)** — later replaced by the **Competition Act, 2002**.
- **De-reservation** of sectors earlier reserved for the public sector.

## Privatisation

- **Disinvestment**: sale of government equity in PSEs via IPO/offer-for-sale (minority stake) or **strategic sale** (transfer of control).
- **Department of Disinvestment created in 1999**; landmark strategic sales — **BALCO, VSNL**.

## Trade & financial reforms

- **Tariff cuts and removal of quantitative restrictions**; **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** to boost exports.
- **SEBI established in 1992** as capital-market regulator.
- **Narasimham Committee** reforms in banking — cut in **SLR/CRR**, Basel norms, more competition.
- Later steps: **GST (2017)**, faceless assessment, four **Labour Codes (2019–20)**.

## Terms explained

- **Industrial licensing** — the old permit system a firm needed before producing (mostly abolished in 1991).
- **Disinvestment** — the government selling part of its stake in a public-sector company.
- **Strategic sale** — selling a controlling stake so management passes to a private buyer.
- **SEZ** — Special Economic Zone: an export enclave with tax and customs benefits.

## TL;DR

- Industrial licensing abolished for most industries; only a few strategic sectors retained licences.
- MRTP Act amended (1991), later replaced by the Competition Act, 2002.
- Disinvestment = sale of government stake in PSEs; Department of Disinvestment set up in 1999 (BALCO, VSNL sold).
- Trade reforms: tariff cuts, removal of quantitative restrictions, and Special Economic Zones (SEZs).
- SEBI established in 1992; Narasimham Committee guided banking reforms (SLR/CRR cuts, Basel norms).

items.title: Balance of Payments — Structure & Convertibility
items.body:
## In one line

The **Balance of Payments** is the country's full account of money coming in and going out across its borders. Asked for its three sub-accounts and the current-vs-capital convertibility distinction.

## What the BoP is

The **Balance of Payments** records **all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world** over a period, on a **double-entry** basis. In accounting terms the **overall BoP always balances**; a 'deficit' or 'surplus' refers to a sub-account.

## Three accounts

| Account | What it records |
|---|---|
| **Current** | Merchandise trade, services, income, unilateral transfers (remittances, aid) |
| **Capital** | Capital transfers (debt forgiveness), non-produced non-financial assets (patents) |
| **Financial** | FDI, portfolio investment, reserve assets (forex, gold, SDRs) |

*(An 'Errors and Omissions' entry reconciles data gaps.)*

## Rupee convertibility

- **Current-account convertibility since August 1994** (India accepted IMF Article VIII) — free forex for trade, travel, remittances.
- **Capital-account convertibility is only partial/calibrated**; the **Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006)** gave a phased roadmap.

## Correcting a BoP problem

Export promotion, import substitution, building forex reserves, and prudent fiscal/monetary policy.

## Terms explained

- **Current account** — day-to-day flows: trade in goods, services, income and remittances.
- **Capital & financial account** — investment flows: FDI, portfolio money, loans, reserves.
- **Convertibility** — the freedom to exchange rupees for foreign currency.
- **Double-entry** — every transaction is booked twice (a credit and a debit), so the total always balances.

## TL;DR

- BoP = double-entry record of all transactions between residents and the rest of the world; overall account always balances.
- Current account: merchandise, services, income, unilateral transfers.
- Capital account: capital transfers and non-produced non-financial assets; Financial account: FDI, portfolio, reserve assets.
- Rupee is convertible on current account since August 1994 (IMF Article VIII).
- Capital-account convertibility remains partial; Tarapore Committees (1997, 2006) gave the roadmap.

items.title: FDI vs FPI vs FII, Routes & Sectoral Caps
items.body:
## In one line

This note explains the difference between **foreign money that builds factories (FDI)** and **foreign money that just buys shares (FPI/FII)**, plus who regulates each and the sector caps. A frequent prelims confusion-pair.

## The three foreign-investment types

| Feature | FDI | FPI / FII |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Long-term, in productive assets | Short-term, in financial assets |
| Control | Control/influence over the company | No management control (passive) |
| Volatility | Stable | Volatile ('hot money') |
| Regulator | DPIIT (policy), RBI (FEMA) | SEBI |

*FII is now merged into the broader **FPI** category under SEBI's FPI Regulations, 2019.*

## Framework & routes

- **FEMA, 1999** (replaced FERA 1973) governs foreign exchange; **DPIIT** frames FDI policy.
- Two entry routes: **Automatic** (no prior approval) and **Government/approval** route.
- The **FIPB was abolished in 2017**.

## Sectoral FDI caps (recent)

| Sector | Cap |
|---|---|
| Insurance | 74% (raised from 49% in 2021) |
| Defence | 74% automatic (up to 100% by approval) |
| Telecom | 100% |
| Single-brand retail | 100% automatic |

## Recent trend

Per the **Economic Survey 2023-24**, net FDI fell from **~US$42 bn (FY23) to ~US$26.5 bn (FY24)**; **digital FDI** rose sharply (share 46.6% in FY17 → 69.2% in FY21). Top sources: **Singapore, USA, Mauritius**.

## Terms explained

- **FDI** — Foreign Direct Investment: long-term money that buys/builds productive assets and gives control.
- **FPI / FII** — Foreign Portfolio/Institutional Investment: passive money in shares and bonds, easily withdrawn.
- **FEMA, 1999** — the law governing foreign-exchange dealings (replaced FERA).
- **Automatic vs Government route** — FDI needing no prior approval vs FDI needing approval.

## TL;DR

- FDI = long-term, control, DPIIT/RBI; FPI/FII = short-term, no control, volatile, regulated by SEBI.
- FEMA 1999 (replaced FERA 1973) governs forex; entry via Automatic or Government route; FIPB abolished 2017.
- FDI caps: insurance 74%, defence 74% automatic, telecom 100%, single-brand retail 100%.
- Net FDI fell from ~US$42 bn (FY23) to ~US$26.5 bn (FY24) per Economic Survey 2023-24.
- Digital FDI share rose from 46.6% (FY17) to 69.2% (FY21); top sources Singapore, USA, Mauritius.

items.title: WTO — Structure, Principles & Agreements
items.body:
## In one line

The **World Trade Organization** writes and enforces the rules of global trade; India is a founding member. Asked for its year, principles (MFN, National Treatment) and the main agreements.

## Basics

- The **WTO** was established on **1 January 1995** under the **Marrakesh Agreement (1994)**, succeeding the **GATT** (in force since 1948).
- **HQ: Geneva**; **166 members** (as of 2024); **India is a founding member**; decisions largely by **consensus**.

## Core principles

- **Most-Favoured-Nation (MFN)** — a trade advantage given to one member must be extended to **all** members (no discrimination *between* partners).
- **National Treatment** — imported and domestic goods must be treated **equally** once in the market.

## Major agreements

| Agreement | Subject |
|---|---|
| **AoA** | Agriculture — market access, domestic support, export subsidies |
| **TRIPS** | Intellectual property rights |
| **TRIMS** | Trade-related investment measures |
| **GATS** | Trade in services |
| **SPS** | Sanitary & phytosanitary (food safety, plant/animal health) |

## India's stance

- Defends **public stockholding for food security** (MSP procurement) against AoA subsidy limits.
- Secured the **Peace Clause** at the **Bali Ministerial (2013)** — interim protection until a permanent solution.
- Pushes for lower agri-subsidy pressure on developing countries; the dispute-settlement Appellate Body is currently non-functional.

## Terms explained

- **WTO** — World Trade Organization: the global body that frames and enforces trade rules.
- **GATT** — the earlier General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (1948) that the WTO replaced.
- **MFN (Most-Favoured-Nation)** — a benefit given to one member must go to all members.
- **National Treatment** — foreign and domestic goods are treated equally once imported.

## TL;DR

- WTO established 1 January 1995 (Marrakesh Agreement 1994), succeeding GATT; HQ Geneva; 166 members.
- MFN = no discrimination between trading partners; National Treatment = equal treatment of foreign and domestic goods.
- Key agreements: AoA (agriculture), TRIPS (IP), TRIMS (investment), GATS (services), SPS (health standards).
- India defends public food-stockholding/MSP against AoA subsidy limits.
- Peace Clause agreed at the Bali Ministerial (2013) gives interim protection to food-security stockholding.

items.title: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 & Recent FTAs
items.body:
## In one line

This note covers India's current **Foreign Trade Policy (2023)** and its latest **free-trade agreements** (UAE, Australia, EFTA, UK). High-frequency current affairs — know which deal is with whom and when it came into force.

## Foreign Trade Policy (FTP) 2023

- Came into effect **1 April 2023**; administered by the **Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT)**, Ministry of Commerce.
- **No fixed end date** — a **dynamic, open-ended** policy updated as needed (a break from the earlier 5-year policies).
- **Target: US$2 trillion in exports (goods + services) by 2030.**
- **Four pillars**: incentive-to-remission; export promotion through collaboration; ease of doing business & e-initiatives; emerging areas (**e-commerce exports, districts as export hubs**).
- Introduced **Towns of Export Excellence** and a one-time **amnesty** for export-obligation defaults.

## Recent Free Trade Agreements

| FTA | Partner | In force |
|---|---|---|
| **CEPA** | UAE | 1 May 2022 |
| **ECTA** | Australia | 29 Dec 2022 |
| **TEPA** | EFTA (Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein) | 1 Oct 2025 |
| **CETA** | United Kingdom | 15 Jul 2026 |

- **India–UK CETA**: negotiations concluded 6 May 2025, **signed 24 July 2025**, in force **15 July 2026** — the UK's biggest FTA since Brexit.
- **India–EFTA TEPA**: signed 10 March 2024; carries an **unprecedented US$100 billion investment pledge** over 15 years.
- India **withdrew from RCEP (2019)** over concerns about its trade deficit with China, import surges and dairy-sector protection.

## Terms explained

- **FTP** — Foreign Trade Policy: the government's framework of export-import rules.
- **DGFT** — Directorate General of Foreign Trade, which runs the FTP.
- **FTA** — Free Trade Agreement: a pact cutting tariffs between partner countries.
- **CEPA / ECTA / TEPA / CETA** — India's deals with the UAE / Australia / EFTA / UK.

## TL;DR

- FTP 2023 took effect 1 April 2023 under the DGFT; it is dynamic with no sunset date.
- FTP 2023 targets US$2 trillion of exports (goods + services) by 2030.
- India–UAE CEPA in force May 2022; India–Australia ECTA in force December 2022.
- India–EFTA TEPA (signed March 2024, in force Oct 2025) carries a US$100 bn investment pledge over 15 years.
- India–UK CETA signed 24 July 2025, in force 15 July 2026; India withdrew from RCEP in 2019.

items.title: For Mains — Economic Reforms, Foreign Trade & WTO
items.body:
## In one line

For Mains, this topic is a debate on **openness vs protection**: did liberalisation and global trade integration deliver inclusive growth, and how should India balance WTO rules with food security and strategic autonomy? (Serves mains-4 clauses M4-1, M4-2 and M4-9.)

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes | 1991 BoP crisis, twin deficits, IMF conditionality |
| Features | LPG pillars, FEMA, FTP 2023, WTO agreements, FTAs |
| Significance | Higher growth, IT/services boom, FDI, global value chains |
| Impact | Jobless/uneven growth, agrarian stress, trade-deficit worries |
| Criticism / limits | WTO AoA vs MSP, RCEP exit, FTA concessions |
| Way forward | Second-generation reforms, export diversification, update AoA |

## Data / committees / reports to quote

- **1991:** forex ~US$1.2 bn (2–3 weeks' imports); gold pledge; Narasimham Committee (banking).
- **FDI (Economic Survey 2023-24):** net FDI fell US$42 bn (FY23) → US$26.5 bn (FY24); caps — insurance 74%, defence 74% auto.
- **FTP 2023:** US$2 trillion export target by 2030 (DGFT).
- **FTAs live (Oct 2026):** UAE CEPA (2022), Australia ECTA (2022), **EFTA TEPA (1 Oct 2025, US$100 bn pledge)**, **UK CETA (in force 15 Jul 2026)**; RCEP exit 2019.
- **WTO:** Bali Peace Clause (2013); AoA de minimis 10% on 1986-88 prices.

## AP angle

Liberalisation lifted **AP's IT/pharma and Visakhapatnam port-led industry**, but its farm-dependent economy stays exposed to global price swings; FTAs matter for AP's **seafood and pharma exports**.

## Use in answers

- **Example:** cite the UK CETA (2026) and EFTA TEPA as India's new-generation, investment-linked FTAs.
- **Quote:** reforms were 'growth-enhancing but not sufficiently employment-generating'.
- **Diagram idea:** a timeline from 1991 LPG → WTO 1995 → FTP 2023 → CETA 2026.
